title: A risky business
abstract: Identifying the most pressing societal issues and prioritizing and coordinating action requires contextual judgements about global politics and dynamics and the risk and enabling landscape actors are operating within. What is most important and deserving of action now and into the future? Although the choices are not a zero-sum game—action in one area doesn’t automatically detract from action elsewhere—we cannot simply address every issue we know about with the same urgency, because there are inevitably some, and sometimes fundamental, trade-offs and antagonism in different policy priorities and implementation choices. However, such contextual thinking is typically done tacitly by individuals and organisations as they work towards agendas. This is probably because providing an explicit contextual rationale is challenging, has a substantial subjective component, and is therefore open to being contested. One interesting attempt to snapshot the global risk landscape is the World Economic Forums World Risk Report which, based on a risk perception survey (for the 2024 report 1490 'experts’ across academia, business, government, the international community and civil society, collected from Sept 4 to Oct 9, 2023), attempts to analyse global risks to support decision-makers in balancing current crises and longer-term priorities. The report is essentially an opinion poll about what risks participants believe will be the most impactful in 2024, over the next two years, and over the next 10 years. Perhaps The World Risk Reports greatest strength is that it considers a wide range of factors broadly categorised as economic, environmental, geopolitical, societal, and technological. A “Global risk is defined as the possibility of the occurrence of an event or condition which, if it occurs, would negatively impact a significant proportion of global GDP, population or natural resources”. Over the 19 years that these reports have been published environmental issues have quite dramatically risen up the risk rankings. When asked to select up to five risks that are most likely to present a material crisis on a global scale in 2024 'extreme weather events’ was the most common choice with 66% of participants including it in their top 5 risks. This is perhaps unsurprising given the catalogue of extreme weather-related events in 2023. When asked to estimate the likely impact (severity) of risks over a 2-year period ‘misinformation and disinformation’ rose to the top concern pushing, ‘extreme weather events’ into second place. The remainder of the top 10 were as follows: 3) societal polarization, 4) cyber insecurity, 5) interstate armed conflict, 6) lack of economic opportunity, 7) inflation, 8) involuntary migration, 9) economic downturn, and 10) pollution. Risk severity estimates over a 10-year period, were much more dominated by environmental risks which accounted for all of the top 4 risks; 1) extreme weather events, 2) critical change to earth systems, 3) biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse, 4) natural resource shortages, as well as the 10th 'pollution’. the other top 10 risks over the next 10 years were; 5) misinformation and disinformation, 6) adverse outcomes of AI technologies, 7) involuntary migration, 8) cyber insecurity, and 9) societal polarization. Interestingly there were some disagreements about the urgency of environmental risks, in particular younger respondents tended to rank 'biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse’ and 'critical change to Earth systems’ far more highly over the two-year period compared to older respondents. In tackling environmental risks and their underlying drivers ‘misinformation and disinformation’ and ‘societal polarization’ will be important factors that determine how societies respond to, for example, climate policies and the extent to which scientific evidence is accepted as a reason for change. Like it or not the success or failure of many initiatives will be dependent on approval by increasingly divided and potentially misinformed publics. Tackling misinformation and disinformation without repressive policies and finding broad support for the policies needed will be a key challenge in addressing all of the other risks identified. Assessments like this, imperfect as they must be, are a useful tool in establishing how issues sit within a broader landscape. The 2024 World Risk Report firmly identified environmental risks as top priorities. So far, they are not being treated as such.

title: Predicting malaria outbreaks using earth observation measurements and spatiotemporal deep learning modelling: a South Asian case study from 2000 to 2017
abstract: BACKGROUND: Malaria remains one the leading communicable causes of death. Approximately half of the world's population is considered at risk of infection, predominantly in African and South Asian countries. Although malaria is preventable, heterogeneity in sociodemographic and environmental risk factors over time and across diverse geographical and climatological regions make outbreak prediction challenging. Data-driven approaches accounting for spatiotemporal variability could offer potential for location-specific early warning tools for malaria. METHODS: In this case study, we developed and internally validated a data fusion approach to predict malaria incidence in Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh using geo-referenced environmental factors. For 2000-17, district-level malaria incidence rates for each country were obtained from the US Agency for International Development's Demographic and Health Survey datasets. Environmental factors included average annual temperature, rainfall, and normalised difference vegetation index, obtained from the Advancing Research on Nutrition and Agriculture (known as AReNA) project conducted by the International Food Policy Research Institute in 2020. Data on night-time light intensity was derived from two satellites of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Defense Meteorological Satellite Program-Operational Linescan System: Nighttime Lights Time Series Version 4, and VIIRS Nighttime Day/Night Band Composites version 1. A multi-dimensional spatiotemporal long short-term memory (M-LSTM) model was developed using data from 2000-16 and internally validated for the year 2017. The M-LSTM model consisted of four hidden layers, each with 100 LSTM units; a fully connected layer was used, followed by linear regression, to predict the malaria incidence rate for 2017 using spatiotemporal partitioning. Model performance was measured using accuracy and root mean squared error. Country-specific models were produced for Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan. Bivariate geospatial heatmaps were produced for a qualitative comparison of univariate environmental factors with malaria rates. FINDINGS: for Bangladesh. Bivariate maps showed an inverse relationship between night-time lights and malaria rates; whereas high malaria rates were found in areas with high temperature, rainfall, and vegetation. INTERPRETATION: Malaria outbreaks could be forecasted using remotely measured environmental factors. Modelling techniques that enable simultaneously forecasting ahead in time as well as across large geographical areas might potentially empower regional decision makers to manage outbreaks early. title: Digital planetary health needs ethical guidance
abstract: Digitalisation, the transfer of tasks and dimensions of human life to digital platforms, is causing changes in planetary health. Digital planetary health, as one could call it, has the potential to facilitate the development of healthy, robust, and sustainable societies and regenerative ecosystems.1 Artificial intelligence can track emissions and identify maintenance needs in health-care facilities, leading to a reduced carbon footprint.2 Artificial intelligence can be instrumental in advancing our understanding of energy resources and climate change; it allows us to analyse the complex factors contributing to climate shifts and estimate energy demands for consumers and businesses.
